systems. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission is called to action. Speak directly to responsibilities held by municipal governments. These are not simply matters of awareness. They ask us to examine how our institutions operate and whether Indigenous people can participate in

a specific life with safety, dignity, and a genuine ability to shape decisions. This call to action is especially relevant to our agenda today as we receive a report on systemic barriers, guided by members of the Indigenous Technical Advisory Group. Receiving that guidance is not the end of the work. Reconciliation is a journey of listening, acting, measuring our progress, and remaining accountable to the people who have shared their knowledge and lived experiences with us. It requires humility when our systems fall short.

Through the chair to the committee, I'm pleased to present this report on identifying and addressing systemic barriers within the City of Saskatoon.
Before speaking to the report itself, I want to take a moment to acknowledge the significance of the conversation that informs this work.
The timing of this discussion is meaningful as we recently marked the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
While September 30th provides an important opportunity to reflect, learn and honor the experiences of survivors.
It is also a reminder that reconciliation requires ongoing action.

Between 2023 and January 2025 members of the Indigenous Technical Advisory Group, or I tag, shared their perspectives, experiences, and insights regarding barriers that Indigenous peoples encounter when seeking employment with the City, engaging with us on civic matters, or participating on council appointed boards and committees.
We recognize that providing this feedback required individuals to share lived experiences and observe observations that are not always easy to discuss.
On behalf of administration, I'd like to express our sincere appreciation to the members of I tag for their time, honesty and willingness to help us become a better organization.
The feedback shared has been valuable.
And there's a report represents one example of how administration is working to turn, listening, learning, and relationship building into meaningful action.
This work aligns directly to the Council's reconciliation equity diversity and inclusion or ready council priority area within the 2026-2029 Strategic Plan.
Through that priority area, City Council has identified three outcomes.

Embracing reconciliation is a foundational principle, successfully identifying and removing systemic barriers, oppression, racism, and discrimination, and building a workforce, including leadership that reflects the diversity of Saskatoon's population.
Today's report focuses primarily on the second outcome, which is identifying and removing systemic barriers.
Importantly, this report is not intended to suggest that all barriers have been removed or that this work is complete.
Rather, it demonstrates how administration has listened to the feedback received, what actions have been taken to date, and how this work continues to inform our future priorities and investments.
The report summarizes feedback and actions in three areas, recruitment and retention, public engagement, and participation on council appointed boards and committees.
One of the strongest messages we heard was that meaningful change requires more than policies alone.
It requires ongoing relationship building, cultural understanding, intentional action, and a willingness to examine our own systems and processes.

In recruitment and retention, administration has taken several steps to create more accessible pathways into employment with the city, and to improve the experience of indigenous employees once they join our organization.

This includes the development of an indigenous recruitment strategy, informed by indigenous perspectives, strengthening relationships with indigenous organizations, and educational institutions, establishing indigenous apprenticeship opportunities through partnerships with Saskatoon tribal council, and creating internship and practicum opportunities through Saskatchewan Indian Institute of Technologies.
We've also continued to build awareness and understanding with workforce through training, education and participation in indigenous cultural events.
The creation of the anti advocate position has been an essential, essentially important step in providing support to indigenous employees.
We're also helping non-indigenous employees better understand indigenous cultures, practices, and traditions.

In addition, administration continues to work collaboratively with our civic unions to increase indigenous representation with our workforce through designated opportunities and targeted recruitment efforts.
With respect to public engagement, we heard clearly that engagement is most effective when it is built on trust, relationship and cultural understanding.

To support that work, the city established and filled an indigenous engagement consultant position and continues to leverage indigenous cultural expertise through dedicated resources within the indigenous initiatives department.
These roles help ensure that indigenous voices are engaged earlier, more meaningfully, and ways that respect culture, protocol, and priorities.

We're also continuing to build capacity across the organization, so that engagement with indigenous communities become a shared responsibility rather than the responsibility of a single department or individual within our organization.
Finally, the report highlights opportunities to improve representation within council appointed boards and committees.

The city continues to review governance processes and committee structures to identify opportunities that encourage broader and more inclusive participation by indigenous peoples and other equity deserving groups is important to emphasize that reconciliation and the removal of systemic bears are not projects with a fixed end date.
They require ongoing commitment, continuous learning, and a willingness to adapt as we learn more.
While we are encouraged by the progress reflected in this report, we also recognize that significant work remains ahead.

That is why this work continues to be embedded within the city's strategic plan and why administration is investing time, resources, and organizational effort in the development of a comprehensive reconciliation action plan.

That work, that future work includes addressing systemic barriers across our organization and advancing economic reconciliation initiatives, including increasing indigenous procurement opportunities and fostering stronger economic partnerships with indigenous communities and businesses.
The strategic plan specifically identifies indigenous procurement, indigenous employment, and advancing reconciliation as key measures and actions moving forward.
Ultimately, our goal is not simply to respond to this feedback.
Our goal is to create lasting change by building systems, processes, and relationships that are more inclusive, more equitable, and more reflective of the community we serve.
Again, I would like to thank the members of ITAG for their guidance, their trust and their partnership.
Their contributions have helped advance important conversations, informed meaningful actions, and challenges to continue improving as an organization.

While there is more work ahead, we remain committed to creating a city that works for everyone, and the conditions for all people to feel welcomed, respected, included, and able to thrive in our community.
